v: What a movie!!! Familiar love-story territory becomes something far more sensitive and natural through rooted characters, unforgettable dialogues and beautifully meaningful little songs. Repeated-watch list for sure.
e: C/o Kancharapalem may share a broad emotional space with films like Naa Autograph, but its execution and sensitivity put it well above most comparisons for me. The local setting, first-time actors, natural dialogue and small situational songs create an experience that feels lived-in rather than manufactured — a classic for viewers open to this kind of cinema.
body:
First, thanks to Srikanth Dontharaju for inspiring — or forcing 😄 — me to watch this movie in a theatre.

Coming to the film itself… what a movie!!!!!

The broad idea may sit in a familiar emotional space alongside films like Naa Autograph and several other stories about love across different phases of life.

But in terms of execution and sensitivity, C/o Kancharapalem is well above most of them for me.

The vintage, rooted neighbourhood backdrop and the wonderfully natural dialogues create an impact that stays with you.

Even a simple exchange can carry enormous emotional weight because the film never feels as though it is trying to manufacture a “cinematic” line.

There are several such scenes and conversations throughout the movie — little moments that become powerful precisely because the characters feel like ordinary people rather than carefully designed film personalities.

The fact that so many of the actors were facing the camera for the first time actually adds to that natural quality.

You are not watching familiar stars performing ordinary people; you feel as though you are watching people from that world simply living their lives.

The short situational songs are another major strength.

They are simple, meaningful and blend beautifully into the atmosphere rather than arriving as commercial interruptions.

This will definitely be on my repeated-watch list once it is available to stream 🙂

P.S. This classic is not really designed for the regular commercial-movie crowd. If this is not your genre, please do not force yourself through it and then kill the soul of the film with expectations it never promised to satisfy 😄

v: Hirani turns Sanju’s own version of the drugs and TADA years into a strong father-son and friendship drama. Ranbir becomes 200% Sanjay Dutt in performance, while Vicky refuses to be overshadowed.
e: Sanju openly presents itself as Sanjay Dutt’s version of events, so I did not see the positive framing as something the film was hiding. By focusing mainly on addiction and the TADA case, Rajkumar Hirani finds enough material to explore the complicated father-son relationship, deep friendship and his familiar criticism of TRP-driven media, backed by an excellent cast.
body:
A lot of people criticised Sanju for showing Sanjay Dutt in a positive light and presenting him as though he were largely a victim.

My first thought was that those viewers may have missed the movie’s very opening setup, which makes it clear that this is Sanju’s version of the incidents.

Coming to the film itself, the plot concentrates mainly on two major chapters — his drug addiction and the TADA case.

That turns out to be enough for Rajkumar Hirani to build strong emotion around the relationship between a superstar father and his spoiled, troubled son, while also exploring the depth of a close friendship.

And in typical Hirani style, he also gives us his take on media houses forever running behind BREAKING NEWS.

The casting is excellent.

Vicky Kaushal, playing Sanju’s best friend, gives such a strong performance that he forces the audience to notice him even while sharing a film with Ranbir Kapoor, Paresh Rawal and Manisha Koirala.

Makeup-wise, Ranbir may resemble about 80% of Sanjay Dutt at various points.

Acting-wise, he becomes 200% Sanjay — especially in the Khalnayak-era portions and during the drug-addiction and rehabilitation sequences 🙏

He completely commits to the mannerisms without allowing the performance to become only mimicry.

The icing on the cake is Sanjay Dutt’s own cameo in the rolling-title song, which doubles down on the film’s criticism of TRP-hungry media.

My very personal disappointment? There was no mention of RGV or Daud — the first movie released after Dutt came out of jail following his first term 😛

That aside, Sanju works very well as the emotional version of the story Hirani chooses to tell.

v: The good news: Pa. Ranjith did not change his storytelling after Kabali. The bad news: exactly the same thing 😄 Apart from a couple of Rajini moments, this tested my patience badly.
e: Kaala doubles down on Pa. Ranjith’s preferred style even though that approach had already frustrated me in Kabali. The film rarely feels like a Rajinikanth vehicle, the exaggerated supporting characterisations and recurring rap interventions became exhausting, and even Nana Patekar is given a generic role — for me, Kabali was considerably better.
body:
The GOOD thing is that Pa. Ranjith did not change his style of storytelling after Kabali.

And the WORST thing is… Pa. Ranjith did not change his style of storytelling after Kabali!!!!! 😄

Rajinikanth may have accepted Kaala because the story and its social angle could help him connect strongly with the masses, particularly at a time when he was considering a political future.

But as a movie fan, I felt that decision came at the cost of torturing a large section of his film audience.

Apart from perhaps two scenes, this barely felt like a Rajini movie to me.

Many earlier Rajinikanth films carried strong social messages while still wrapping them inside commercial elements that made terrific use of his screen presence.

Here, Pa. Ranjith seems far more concerned with his own storytelling style and a collection of exaggerated characterisations that repeatedly tested my patience.

Special mention has to go to the RAP gang that appears to stay beside Kaala irrespective of the situation and rap its way through everything.

Even moments that should carry grief or tension are interrupted by these performances, and after a point I was simply exhausted by the creative choice 🙏

Nana Patekar is wasted in a fairly generic role, although he is such a strong performer that he still makes his presence felt whenever he appears.

Ultimately, if I have to compare the experience with Pa. Ranjith’s previous Rajini film, Kabali was far better than Kaala for me.

v: Go in with an open mind and Officer has plenty to like: a focused cop-vs-corrupt-cop story, realistic action, superb BGM and an RGV visual style that refuses normal commercial hero rules.
e: Officer is deliberately far removed from conventional star cinema: Nagarjuna’s cop runs when survival demands it, there is no standard heroine track or hero-elevation package, the violence is harsh and RGV’s odd camera angles remain unapologetically his own. Those choices will alienate many viewers, but I liked the focused two-hour conflict, intelligent action design, BGM and several sharp dialogues.
body:
Before talking about Officer itself, I think part of the disastrous word of mouth around it had very little to do with the actual film.

RGV’s recent off-screen attitude had rubbed many people the wrong way, and a section of the audience — including some reviewers — seemed determined to declare the movie a disaster even before release.

The second problem is that the film is intentionally realistic in ways that clash with regular hero expectations.

When Nagarjuna’s cop is in danger, he actually runs for his life and waits for the right opportunity instead of magically fighting five hundred goons.

The violence is also genuinely harsh in places, which makes the movie unsuitable for sensitive or family audiences.

And, of course, RGV continues using those strange camera angles that can be uncomfortable for viewers accustomed to conventional framing.

Now to the common complaint that the film has “no story.”

Were those people sleeping in the theatre? 😄

The film is only about two hours long and focuses on the conflict between a police officer who is secretly operating as a mafia leader and another officer who becomes falsely framed as part of that criminal world.

How much more plot does a focused two-hour action film really need?

Yes, Officer stays far away from typical commercial ingredients.

There is no conventional heroine track, no giant hero-elevation scenes and no endless punch-dialogue package.

Instead, the protagonist behaves like an actual vulnerable human being, and the female lead even fires more bullets than the hero in places 🙏

The movie still contains several thought-provoking lines about power, truth, enemies and the good and evil inside every person.

I do agree that RGV should eventually move beyond his endless fascination with underworld and mafia stories.

But for this film, he and Nagarjuna had repeatedly promised realistic, intelligent action and strong sound design — and they deliver that.

The BGM is excellent, while the beach sequence, Essel World episode and climax contain some of the better action staging in the movie.

I may have connected with Officer partly because I am an ardent RGV fan and his visual style has even influenced the way I take photographs.

But my wife and daughter liked the film as well.

So I would simply say this: go with an open mind and there is a fair chance you may enjoy it too.
